title: An initial study to test whether patients can tolerate preventative VACStent treatment started during surgery to remove the oesophagus, with the aim of reducing leaks where the remaining oesophagus and stomach are joined together
official: Prophylactic stenting at time of oesophagectomy using VACStent: a pilot study
summary:
Background and study aims
Surgery to remove part or most of the oesophagus (food pipe), known as an oesophagectomy, is a key treatment for potentially curable oesophageal cancer. It may also involve removing the upper part of the stomach and is usually combined with other cancer treatments.

Oesophagectomy is major surgery with a high risk of complications. One of the most serious is an *anastomotic leak*, which occurs when the join between the remaining oesophagus and stomach leaks. This affects around 10–15% of patients and can cause severe illness because stomach contents leak into the chest, close to the heart. Early recognition and treatment are important to improve outcomes.

Treatment depends on the severity of the leak and may involve antibiotics, procedures performed using a flexible camera (endoscopy), or further surgery. Patients may require care in a critical care unit. Anastomotic leak usually prolongs hospital stay and increases the risk of death within 90 days of oesophagectomy. 

Three endoscopic procedures are commonly used in treating anastomotic leak:
1) Stenting: A hollow tube is placed across the leak to prevent further leakage and allow healing. Patients can often drink some liquids.
2) Endoscopic vacuum therapy (EVT): A sponge attached to a tube is placed at the leak and connected to a vacuum pump to encourage healing and control infection. Patients cannot eat or drink and receive nutrition through a feeding tube or directly into their bloodstream.  The sponge is changed every 3–5 days until the leak has healed.
3) VAC-Stenting: This combines a stent with vacuum therapy to prevent further leakage, control infection and promote healing. Patients can often drink some liquids, and the device is changed every 7 days.

Given the serious consequences of anastomotic leaks, better treatments and ways to prevent anastomotic leak are needed. This study will investigate whether using VAC-Stenting preventatively for seven days after oesophagectomy can reduce the risk of anastomotic leak. Although VAC-Stenting is already used to treat leaks, using it to prevent them is a new approach. Before it can be evaluated in larger studies, a smaller study is needed to ensure it does not pose additional risks to patients. The main aim is to assess whether preventative VAC-Stenting is safe and can be tolerated for the intended duration. The study will also measure the rate of anastomotic leaks and other surgical outcomes.

Who can participate?
Patients aged 18 years or older diagnosed with oesophageal cancer who have a plan for surgery to remove the oesophagus (oesophagectomy)

What does the study involve?
Eligible participants who consent to take part in the study are all allocated to receive a VACStent at the time of oesophagectomy.  Once the tumour has been surgically removed and the stomach has been joined to the remaining oesophagus (anastomosis), an upper GI endoscopy will be carried out while still in theatre under general anaesthetic.  A VAC-Stent will be placed across the anastomosis.  This will be connected to a vacuum pump via a tube exiting the body from the nose.  The VACStent will be left in place for up to 7 days.  We will analyse how well VACStent therapy is tolerated and any complications related to the VACstent (if any).  At the end of the study (30 days after surgery) we will record any postoperative complications including anastomotic leak and what treatment (if any) was given for these as well as the number of days between surgery and discharge from hospital.  

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
The use of a prophylactic VAC-Stent could potentially prevent an anastomotic leak and the its associated adverse impact as discussed above.  In addition, this study will help to inform larger studies, which may result in a change in the care we routinely provide to patients to include prophylactic measures such as VACStent therapy to help prevent anastomotic leak.  

An upper GI endoscopy will be required to remove the VACStent after 7 days. This will be an additional procedure to the normal care pathway, but will enable the anastomosis to be directly visualised to assess how healthy and patent it is and ensure there is no visual evidence of anastomotic leak.  
  
Participation in this study includes some risks.  These have been carefully considered, and processes have been developed to minimise these and their impact on participants and carers.  Any medical device we use can have technical problems in addition to the complications associated with the procedure and therapy.  Information relating to specific risks of VACStent therapy is outlined in the Patient Information Sheet and should be discussed with your doctor or a member of the care team.

Where is the study run from?
University of Dundee (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
November 2026 until April 2028

conditions: Prevention of anastomotic leak in patients undergoing oesophagectomy

interventions.name: Eligible participants who have provided informed consent will undergo insertion of a VACStent to cover the oesophagogastric anastomosis at the time of surgery. All anastomoses (whether open or laparoscopic) will be carried out using a standardised technique of linear stapled oesophagogastric anastom

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. 18 years of age or older 
2. Willing and able to provide written informed consent
3. Pathologically proven adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus or oesophageal junction 
4. Regional MDT: suitable for oesophagectomy 
5. ECOG performance status 0-1
6. BMI ≥ 22.0kg/m²
Exclusion criteria:
1. Patient not eligible for oesophagectomy 
2. Patients requiring treatment dose anticoagulation
3. Patients undergoing oesophagectomy with cervical anastomosis 
4. Metastatic disease 
5. Any significant medical condition that in the opinion of the Principal Investigator (PI) would impair the ability of the participant to complete the requirements of the protocol
6. Known allergy or hypersensitivity to any of the components of the VACStent material
7. Patients with nasal deformity preventing insertion of nasal tube
8. Previous radiotherapy to the thorax / oesophagus
